checkpoints: Kafka gives only at-least-once delivery: offsets commit after a message is successfully handled, so a consumer crash or restart resumes from the last committed offset and redelivers messages that were already processed.
A handler that writes to an external store on every message must be idempotent — safe to run again on a message it already applied, without throwing or corrupting state.

`es.create` maps to Elasticsearch's create-only `PUT /_create/<id>` operation, which throws a 409 conflict if a document with that id already exists, so replaying an already-indexed `c`/`u`/`r` message crashes the handler.
`es.delete` throws a 404 when the target id no longer exists, and with no try/catch around the call, replaying an already-processed `d` message also crashes the handler.

`es.index` is a PUT-by-id operation that overwrites whatever document currently holds that id (or creates it if absent), so calling it repeatedly with the same id and payload is a genuinely idempotent upsert, unlike `es.create`.

Folding the three ops `c`/`u`/`r` into a single `es.index({ index, id, document: after })` call, and wrapping `es.delete({ index, id })` in a `.catch(() => undefined)` to swallow 404s, makes the handler safe to reprocess any number of times and converges on the same final document per id.

Diagnosing this kind of bug should start from naming the delivery guarantee that causes redelivery in the first place, then trace down to the two specific non-idempotent calls, before proposing the fix — jumping straight to a code patch skips the actual root cause.

Correctness should be verified by actually replaying already-processed messages (restarting the consumer or resending them) and confirming no exception is thrown and each id ends up with exactly one document holding the latest data, with no duplicates.
